description: Original new-language expansion. Expected outputs are development checks and are not bundled as grading rules.

lessons.title: A type parameter keeps relationships explicit
lessons.summary: Reuse one definition without erasing its types.
body: A generic definition names a type parameter instead of choosing one concrete type. The same parameter in several positions means those positions must agree for a particular call.
The body must work under the declared constraints. An unconstrained T cannot be compared or printed just because the eventual caller uses integers.
Returning Option<&T> lets this function borrow an element and represent an empty slice without copying it. The borrow still obeys the input's lifetime.
lessons.challenge: Write a generic second function that returns None when the slice has fewer than two elements.
lessons.question: Without a trait bound, what must the body of a generic function assume about T?
options: Only the operations permitted by its declared constraints
That every T can be printed
That T has a default constructor
lessons.explanation: The compiler checks the generic definition under its declared constraints, rather than assuming the capabilities of a particular caller's type.
recall: Why repeat the same type parameter in several positions?
It expresses a type relationship: those positions use the same chosen type in a particular call.
Why return Option<&T> from a slice lookup?
It represents absence and borrows the element without requiring it to be copied.

lessons.title: A trait bound states the required behavior
lessons.summary: Separate an interface from a particular representation.
body: A trait names behavior that implementing types provide. Implementing the trait for a type supplies those methods; it does not require that the type inherit a data layout.
A generic trait bound such as T: Weight allows the body to call the trait's methods. This is a useful bridge from C# interfaces and C++ constrained templates.
The function below borrows each parcel. Computing its weight does not consume the parcel, and different implementations can supply the same interface.
lessons.challenge: Implement Weight for a Crate whose weight includes both its contents and its packaging.
lessons.question: What does T: Weight allow the generic total function to do?
options: Read every private field of T
Call the behavior required by Weight
Treat T as a subclass of Parcel
lessons.explanation: The bound supplies the trait contract; it does not expose an implementing type's fields or bypass ownership rules.
recall: What does a trait bound give a generic function?
A declared set of capabilities that the function can rely on.
Does implementing a Rust trait imply shared field layout?
No. Types can implement the same behavior with different representations.

lessons.title: Iterator adapters wait for a consumer
lessons.summary: Choose borrowing, mutation, or ownership before chaining.
body: Iterator adapters such as map and filter build a lazy computation. A consumer such as collect or sum asks it to produce results.
For a Vec, iter borrows elements, iter_mut borrows them mutably, and into_iter takes ownership of the vector's elements. Choose that relationship before writing a pipeline.
Here copied turns borrowed integers into copied values. The original vector remains available because the pipeline began with iter.
lessons.challenge: Use iter_mut to double every element in place, then print the updated vector.
lessons.question: For a Vec<T>, which iterator takes ownership of its elements?
lessons.explanation: Calling into_iter on the owned vector consumes it; iter and iter_mut borrow instead.
recall: What makes an iterator adapter run its computation?
A consumer requests elements, for example through collect, sum, or a loop.
How do Vec iter and into_iter differ?
iter borrows elements; into_iter on the owned vector consumes it and yields owned elements.

lessons.title: A lifetime annotation describes a borrow relationship
body: A lifetime parameter relates references in a signature. It tells the checker which input borrows constrain an output borrow; it does not keep an object alive for longer.
When either input might be returned, the caller must be able to use both inputs for the lifetime required by the returned reference. The annotation expresses that shared constraint.
Many simple signatures use lifetime elision. Adding annotations cannot make a reference to a local temporary safe to return.
lessons.challenge: Write a first_word function borrowing from one input. Let lifetime elision connect the result to that input.
lessons.question: Can a lifetime annotation extend the life of a local String so a reference to it can be returned?
options: Yes, if the result is a string slice
No; it describes constraints rather than extending storage
lessons.explanation: An annotation cannot prevent the local value from being dropped when its scope ends.
recall: What does a Rust lifetime annotation describe?
Relationships and validity constraints between borrowed references.
Why can annotations not fix returning a reference to a local value?
The local value is dropped; annotations do not extend its storage lifetime.

lessons.title: Move transfers data; join waits for work
body: A spawned thread can outlive the scope that started it. An ordinary spawned closure therefore needs captures that meet the thread API's lifetime and Send requirements.
A move closure takes ownership of captures such as this vector. That solves the capture's ownership problem, but does not wait for the thread to finish.
Joining waits for completion and returns a Result containing the thread's returned value or panic information. Here the main thread prints only after joining, making the output deterministic.
lessons.challenge: Move a vector to a worker that counts even values. Join it and print the count.
lessons.question: Which operation waits for the spawned thread's completion?
lessons.explanation: move determines how captures enter the closure; join supplies the synchronization with completion.
recall: Does a move closure wait for its thread?
No. It determines capture ownership; join waits for completion.
What does a thread JoinHandle's join return?
A Result with the returned value on success or panic information on failure.

lessons.title: Turn an expected behavior into a check
lessons.summary: Use assertions while keeping test scope honest.
body: An assertion checks a concrete behavior and panics when the expectation fails. Check boundary cases as well as an ordinary happy path.
Rust's unit-test harness normally discovers functions marked #[test] through cargo test or rustc --test. Running a main program alone does not run those test functions.

The mobile lab currently runs a single program. These examples put assertions in main so the current execution contract actually exercises them. Passing selected cases still does not prove the function correct for every input.
lessons.challenge: Write a slice total and check both an empty slice and a non-empty slice before printing success.
lessons.question: Does running a normal main program automatically execute every #[test] function?
options: No; the test harness must be used
Only for tests in the same file
lessons.explanation: The ordinary program entry point and Rust's test harness are separate execution paths.
recall: Why include boundary cases in tests?
They check behavior where ordinary inputs may miss bugs, such as empty collections or exact thresholds.
What is the difference between passing tests and a general proof?
Tests check selected cases; a proof establishes a stated proposition under its definitions and assumptions.

lessons.title: Record update creates a new value
lessons.summary: Name fields while making changes explicit.
body: A record groups named fields with declared types. Fields are immutable unless their declaration explicitly marks them mutable.
The with syntax constructs a new record using existing fields as defaults. It does not mutate the original record.
This is a shallow update: if a field refers to mutable storage, that storage can still be shared. Here both the integer and string fields are immutable values.
lessons.challenge: Write extend that returns a session with five extra minutes, leaving the input value unchanged.
lessons.question: What does { original with minutes = 15 } do for this immutable record?
options: Create a new record with that field replaced
lessons.explanation: Record update builds a new record; it does not promise a deep copy of any referenced mutable values.
recall: Are OCaml record fields mutable by default?
No. A field must explicitly be declared mutable.
Does an OCaml record update deep-copy referenced storage?
No. It constructs a new record while retaining the other field values, which may refer to shared storage.

lessons.title: A type variable connects a function's positions
body: A polymorphic function can be used with different concrete types at different calls. Repeating a type variable within one function type records a relationship between positions.
For apply_twice, the argument function must return the same type that it accepts, because its first result becomes its next input.
Type inference is static checking, not a request to treat values as dynamically typed. Some definitions, particularly those involving mutable state, face restrictions on generalization.
lessons.challenge: Write compose f g x = f (g x), then compose String.length with String.uppercase_ascii.
lessons.question: Which type fits apply_twice f x = f (f x)?
options: Every argument has an unrelated type
lessons.explanation: The output of f is used as another input to f, so those two types must agree.
recall: What does a repeated OCaml type variable express?
The corresponding positions share the same chosen type within that use of the function.
Why must f accept and return the same type in apply_twice?
The first result is passed to f again.

lessons.title: The accumulator carries the computation
lessons.summary: Trace a fold instead of guessing its order.
body: A fold combines each list element with an accumulator. fold_left passes the current accumulator first; fold_right passes the current element first.
For non-associative operations such as subtraction, direction and argument order change the result. Write out the nested calls when reasoning about them.
Building a list by prepending to a fold_left accumulator reverses the order. Use that deliberately rather than assuming every fold preserves order.
lessons.code:
let values = [1; 2; 3]
let left = List.fold_left ( - ) 0 values
let right = List.fold_right ( - ) values 0
let () = Printf.printf "%d %d\n" left right
lessons.challenge: Implement reverse with List.fold_left and ::, then print the reversed values separated by commas.
lessons.question: Which calculation describes List.fold_left ( - ) 0 [1; 2; 3]?
lessons.explanation: fold_left threads the accumulator from the left, making each intermediate result the next first argument.
recall: Which argument receives the accumulator in fold_left's combining function?
The first argument.
Why can fold_left and fold_right differ for subtraction?
Their nesting and argument order differ, and subtraction is not associative.

lessons.title: A signature can hide a representation
lessons.summary: Expose operations while keeping a type abstract.
body: A module groups types and values. A signature describes what clients may see and use.
Writing type t in a signature without revealing its definition makes the representation abstract outside that interface. Clients must use the exported constructors and operations.
The implementation below uses int, but a client cannot assume Counter.t is int. This lets the implementation change while preserving its public contract.
lessons.code:
module Counter : sig
  type t
  val zero : t
  val next : t -> t
  val value : t -> int
end = struct
  type t = int
  let zero = 0
  let next n = n + 1
  let value n = n
end
let () = Printf.printf "%d\n" (Counter.value (Counter.next Counter.zero))
lessons.challenge: Add a reset operation to the signature and implementation, then reset an incremented counter.
lessons.solution:
module Counter : sig
  type t
  val zero : t
  val next : t -> t
  val reset : t -> t
  val value : t -> int
end = struct
  type t = int
  let zero = 0
  let next n = n + 1
  let reset _ = zero
  let value n = n
end
let () =
  let count = Counter.next (Counter.next Counter.zero) in
  Printf.printf "%d\n" (Counter.value (Counter.reset count))
lessons.question: Can a client pass the integer 3 directly to Counter.value through this abstract signature?
options: Yes, because the implementation uses int
No, because Counter.t is abstract to the client
lessons.explanation: The exported signature hides the equality between Counter.t and int.
recall: What does an abstract type in a module signature hide?
Its concrete representation and any type equality that has not been exposed.
How can clients create values of an abstract type?
Through operations exported by the signature, such as zero or a constructor function.

lessons.title: A functor takes a module as its input
body: An OCaml functor maps a module satisfying an input signature to a result module. This is different from a map operation on a collection.
Use a functor when several definitions should depend on the same supplied types or operations. The module signature specifies the required dependency.
Here two applications can provide different offsets while reusing the implementation. The returned modules have their own exported names.
lessons.code:
module type Offset = sig val amount : int end
module Shift (O : Offset) = struct
  let apply n = n + O.amount
end
module PlusFive = Shift (struct let amount = 5 end)
let () = Printf.printf "%d\n" (PlusFive.apply 7)
lessons.challenge: Apply Shift twice to produce PlusTwo and PlusTen, then apply both to 7.
lessons.solution:
module type Offset = sig val amount : int end
module Shift (O : Offset) = struct
  let apply n = n + O.amount
end
module PlusTwo = Shift (struct let amount = 2 end)
module PlusTen = Shift (struct let amount = 10 end)
let () = Printf.printf "%d %d\n" (PlusTwo.apply 7) (PlusTen.apply 7)
lessons.question: What is the input to Shift in this example?
lessons.explanation: Shift is a functor whose parameter is a module exposing amount : int.
recall: What does an OCaml functor accept and return?
It accepts a module matching a signature and produces a module.
Why use a module parameter rather than pass one value to every function?
It groups shared type/operation dependencies so several definitions can use the same contract.

lessons.title: Expected failures can travel as values
body: The result type distinguishes Ok carrying a success value from Error carrying a failure value. Pattern matching makes the two paths visible.
For an expected validation failure, returning a result lets a caller choose how to report or recover. Exceptions remain useful for other error-handling designs.
Result.map changes the successful value and preserves an Error. Result.bind is for a next operation that can itself return a result.
lessons.challenge: Double a valid parsed number using Result.map while preserving an invalid input's Error.
lessons.question: What does Result.map do when its input is Error message?
options: Run the mapping function on message
Preserve the Error without mapping the success value
lessons.explanation: The mapping function applies only to the Ok branch.
recall: How do result's two constructors differ?
Ok carries a success value; Error carries a failure value.
When use Result.bind rather than Result.map?
Use bind when the next successful step can itself return a result and fail.

lessons.title: Pattern matching follows the constructors
lessons.summary: Compute by handling every shape of an input.
body: An inductive type describes values through constructors. Nat has zero and successor cases; pattern matching gives the computation for each case.
The successor pattern n + 1 binds the predecessor n. It is a pattern for a natural number's constructor shape, not a general equation solver.
Recursive calls must satisfy Lean's termination requirements. Structural recursion on the predecessor is a natural starting point before proving properties about a recursive definition.
lessons.code:
def remaining : Nat → Nat
  | 0 => 0
  | n + 1 => n
#eval remaining 4
lessons.challenge: Define twiceBySteps recursively: return 0 at zero and add 2 for each successor. Evaluate it at 3.
lessons.solution:
def twiceBySteps : Nat → Nat
  | 0 => 0
  | n + 1 => 2 + twiceBySteps n
#eval twiceBySteps 3
lessons.question: In the successor pattern n + 1, what does n represent?
options: The predecessor of the matched natural number
lessons.explanation: The branch receives the predecessor from the successor constructor.
recall: What cases are needed to pattern-match on Nat?
Zero and successor.
Why is recursion on the predecessor a useful Lean starting point?
It follows the inductive structure and supplies a structurally smaller recursive argument.

lessons.title: Conjunction needs evidence for both sides
lessons.summary: Build and use a pair of proofs.
body: A proof of P ∧ Q contains evidence for P and evidence for Q. Given h : P ∧ Q, h.1 and h.2 select those two proofs.
To construct a conjunction, supply both components, for example ⟨hp, hq⟩. In tactic mode, constructor creates the corresponding subgoals.
A conjunction differs from a disjunction: proving P ∨ Q requires choosing and proving one side, while a conjunction needs both.
lessons.code:
theorem swapBoth (P Q : Prop) : P ∧ Q → Q ∧ P := by
  intro h
  exact ⟨h.2, h.1⟩
lessons.challenge: Prove P → Q → P ∧ Q by introducing both assumptions and constructing the conjunction.
lessons.solution:
theorem keepBoth (P Q : Prop) : P → Q → P ∧ Q := by
  intro hp hq
  exact ⟨hp, hq⟩
lessons.question: Given h : P ∧ Q, which term proves Q?
options: A proof of either side chosen at random
lessons.explanation: The second projection selects the proof of Q from the conjunction.
recall: What evidence is needed to prove P ∧ Q?
A proof of P and a proof of Q.
How does conjunction differ from disjunction when constructing evidence?
Conjunction needs both sides; disjunction needs a selected side and its proof.

lessons.title: A universal proof can be applied
lessons.summary: Distinguish evidence for every input from one witness.
body: A proof of ∀ n, P n behaves like a function taking n and returning evidence for P n. Apply it to a particular argument to get the corresponding proof.
An existential proof, ∃ n, P n, instead packages one witness together with evidence that the witness satisfies P.
When introducing a universal variable, it is arbitrary: checking a few numerical examples does not establish the universally quantified proposition.
lessons.code:
theorem atFive (P : Nat → Prop) (hEvery : ∀ n, P n) : P 5 := by
  exact hEvery 5
lessons.challenge: From h : P 4, construct a proof that there exists a natural number satisfying P.
lessons.solution:
theorem hasWitness (P : Nat → Prop) (h : P 4) : ∃ n, P n := by
  exact ⟨4, h⟩
lessons.question: What must be supplied to construct a proof of ∃ n, P n?
options: A witness n and evidence for P n
The type Nat without a value
A list of tested values without proofs
lessons.explanation: The existential constructor packages a particular witness with the proof of its property.
recall: How do you use h : ∀ n, P n to prove P 5?
Apply h to 5.
What does evidence for an existential proposition contain?
A witness and a proof that the witness satisfies the stated property.

lessons.title: An equality can change the current goal
lessons.summary: Choose the direction of a rewrite.
body: Given h : a = b, rw [h] rewrites matching occurrences of a to b. The reverse direction, rw [← h], uses b = a.
Inspect the goal before and after a rewrite. Rewriting uses an equality theorem; it does not assert that every mathematically equal expression is definitionally identical.
If the transformed sides coincide, reflexivity can close the goal. For larger expressions, more rewrites or simplification may still be needed.
lessons.code:
example (a b : Nat) (h : a = b) : a + 2 = b + 2 := by
  rw [h]
lessons.challenge: Use h : a = b in the reverse direction to prove b + 3 = a + 3.
lessons.solution:
example (a b : Nat) (h : a = b) : b + 3 = a + 3 := by
  rw [← h]
lessons.question: What is the direction of rw [← h] when h : a = b?
lessons.explanation: The left arrow requests the symmetric direction of the supplied equality.
recall: How do you request the reverse direction of a Lean rewrite?
Use rw [← h] for the equality h.
How does rewriting differ from definitional equality?
Rewriting uses an equality proof; definitional equality comes from Lean's reductions.

lessons.title: Induction mirrors a recursive definition
lessons.summary: Use a smaller case to prove the next case.
body: Induction on a natural number creates a zero case and a successor case. In the successor case, the induction hypothesis describes the proposition for the predecessor.
A recursive function's defining equations often determine the proof steps: unfold the current case, use the induction hypothesis, and simplify.
The induction hypothesis is a proof for the smaller case, not permission to assume the final theorem for every value. Check the exact hypothesis and remaining goal.
lessons.code:
def tally : Nat → Nat
  | 0 => 0
  | n + 1 => tally n + 1
theorem tallySelf (n : Nat) : tally n = n := by
  induction n with
  | zero => rfl
  | succ n ih => simp [tally, ih]
#eval tally 4
lessons.challenge: Define zeros n as a list of n zeroes and prove that its length is n by induction.
lessons.solution:
def zeros : Nat → List Nat
  | 0 => []
  | n + 1 => 0 :: zeros n
theorem zerosLength (n : Nat) : (zeros n).length = n := by
  induction n with
  | zero => rfl
  | succ n ih => simp [zeros, ih]
#eval (zeros 3).length
lessons.question: In the successor case of this induction, what does ih describe?
options: The proposition for the predecessor n
lessons.explanation: The induction principle supplies evidence for the smaller case, which is used to prove the successor case.
recall: What two cases arise from induction on Nat?
Zero and successor, with an induction hypothesis for the predecessor in the successor case.
Why can a recursive definition guide an induction proof?
Its cases identify how to reduce the expression and where the smaller-case hypothesis applies.

lessons.title: A structure groups named fields
lessons.summary: Build a value and project its components.
body: A structure groups fields under a named type. Lean generates a constructor and field projections; dot notation lets you access fields from a value.
Record update constructs a new structure value with selected fields replaced. The original immutable value remains available.
Fields can also include proof obligations, but plain Nat fields do not automatically enforce a relationship such as completed ≤ total. State and prove an invariant when your design requires it.
lessons.code:
structure Progress where
  completed : Nat
  total : Nat
def start : Progress := { completed := 2, total := 5 }
#eval start.completed
lessons.challenge: Define advance returning a new Progress with completed incremented. Check the old and new counts.
lessons.question: Does this Progress declaration by itself guarantee completed ≤ total?
options: Yes, because both fields are Nat
No; the relationship needs its own constraint or proof
Yes, because it is a structure
lessons.explanation: The field types restrict each value individually but do not impose the relationship between the fields.
recall: What does Lean generate for a structure declaration?
A constructor, field projections, and supporting eliminators/theorems.
How can a Lean structure express an invariant beyond field types?
Include a corresponding proof field or establish the invariant through separate definitions and theorems.
